en: Padminī Ratnarakṣita Chapter 32

Now, in order to answer the question, "O Lord, how is the *alibali* [offering] performed?", he says "atha" and so forth. "Maṇḍala" refers to the time of beginning the drawing of the maṇḍala, the fire sacrifice (*homa*), the recitation (*japa*), and so on. "*Alibali*" means an offering (*bali*) joined with *ali*, which is a liquid substance; it is performed even without that. "Protection" (*rakṣā*) refers to the two armor-mantras (*kavaca*) of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady. "Resounded by the sound of the syllable *hūṃ*" means preceded by the utterance of the three syllables. "Instantly" (*jhaṭiti*) is said with reference to the practitioner who meditates according to the *utpannakrama* (the stage of completion). "Mantra" refers to *oṃ sarvavīra* and so forth.

In order to provide an answer to the question, "How is the intoxicating *bali* offering the most important?", it is said, beginning with "Then," and so forth. "Mandala" refers to the time of undertaking the drawing of the mandala, the fire offering (*homa*), the recitation (*japa*), and so on. "Intoxicating *bali* offering" means [the offering] lacking the *bali* substance consisting of liquor and semen.

"Protection" refers to the two armors of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady. "Proclaiming the sound of the syllable HŪṂ" means preceded by the recitation of the three syllables. "Instantly" is said in relation to the practitioner of the completion stage and others. "Mantra" refers to *oṃ sarvavīra* and so forth.

This is the meaning: at the beginning of the commencement of meditation and in all such instances, one should immediately, preceded by the yoga of the two-armed Samvara, recite: "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ! I am of the nature of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all heroes and yoginīs."

Having recited the mantra, *oṃ vajraśuddhāḥ sarvadharmā vajraśuddho ’ham*, one should immediately resolve upon the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), as well as the two armors (*kavaca*). One should then clearly visualize the entire assembly without exception—the twenty-four heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*), and so forth—at the twenty-four locations on the body. Having worshipped the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) as prescribed within a mandala prepared with fragrant substances and other offerings in front of oneself, he asks what should be done next; thus he says, "First," and so forth. This is easily understood.

The passage beginning with *samayas tvam* and ending with *devatāṃ tarpayet* is to be understood as following immediately after the phrase *yathāsukham*. This is the meaning: in all instances, such as when commencing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should first perform the yoga of the two-armed Saṃvara for a single moment, [reciting]: oṃ āḥ hūṃ sarvavīrayoginīnāṃ kāyavākcittavajrasvabhāvātmako ’haṃ | oṃ vajraśuddhaḥ sarvadharmā vajraśuddho ’haṃ ||

Having recited these three mantras, in an instant one should cultivate intense conviction that the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are completely pure, and that upon the two types of armor and the twenty-four sites of the body, the twenty-four lords of heroes and heroines, and so forth, are present without exception. Then, having prepared a maṇḍala with fragrant substances and the like in front [of oneself],...

Having correctly worshipped the divine wheel exactly as it is, how should one proceed? It is said: "At the beginning," and so forth, which is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "samayas tvam" and so on, up until the words "devatāḥ prīṇayāmīti," the expression "yathāsukham" should be seen as intervening without interruption.

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: having prepared the *bali* offering according to the stated sequence, one should invoke the Blessed One by means of the *jālāmudrā* and its mantra. Simultaneously, having worshipped Indra and the other deities together with their retinues—beginning with Indra—with the respective mantras and preceded by the *argha* offering and so forth, one should cause them to enter the *samayacakra* as appropriate. Then, holding the *balibhājana* (offering vessel) as a vajra-palms gesture (*vajrāñjali*) born from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated within the hollow formed by one’s own left and right hands—which have the nature of the moon and sun—and having meditated upon it and recited the mantra beginning with "O Samaya... along with the goddesses...

Having recited the verse beginning with "ityādi," one should visualize the deities drinking nectar through tubes of light rays emerging from their tongues, which are vajras with a single prong marked by the syllable *hūṃ*. While rotating them clockwise and counter-clockwise, one should offer the *bali* to the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady, as well as to the *ḍākinīs* and others up to Yamamathani, using the mantra beginning with *oṃ* and the mantra beginning with *oṃ vajra*. Then, the passage beginning with "tata ityādi" is easy to understand.
Having offered betel and so forth collectively with the eight-line mantra, one should praise the Blessed Lord and pray for the desired outcome, such as pacification (*śānti*) and the like.

The meaning of this is as follows: having prepared the *bali* offering according to the stated sequence, one should invoke the Blessed One with the *jāla-mudrā* and its mantra; at that very same time, one should [invoke] Indra and the others, together with their retinues, using the mantra beginning with "Aindra."

Having performed the offerings, such as the *argha* water, preceded by the preliminary rites, one should appropriately introduce [the disciple] into the *samaya*-maṇḍala. Then, having placed or visualized the vessel for the *bali* offering upon the hollow of a vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*, which is formed by the union of one's own left hand and its counterpart, both of which have the nature of the moon and the sun:

While reciting the mantra beginning with *samaya* and the verse beginning with *devī*, one should visualize that nectar is drawn in through the tubes of light rays emanating from the single-pointed vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*, and that the deities partake of it; then, one should circle while rotating the left and the other [right] hands.

With the mantra beginning with *oṃ kara* and so forth, one should offer the *bali* to the Blessed One and the Blessed Lady, as well as to those starting from the ḍākinīs up to Yamamathani, using the mantra beginning with *oṃ vajra* and so forth. Then, and so forth, is easy to understand. "The eight-line [verse]" is also easy to understand.

Having offered tambūla and other items to all [the deities], one should praise the Blessed One with the eight-line mantra and offer prayers for the fulfillment of desired aims, such as peace and so forth.

"Chomma-ka" is the heading; "Oṃ," and so forth, is the detailed explanation. Some say that the *tripatāka* mudrā is the "chomma-hand. Regarding the phrase "after that": it refers to a specific offering of the *utsṛṣṭabali* (discarded oblation) within the context of the *gaṇacakra* (feast gathering).

In this regard, having taken all the foods and condiments contained in the vessel and placed them together in a single container, and having offered flowers, cakes, and so forth, the Ācārya should fill his mouth with *madana* (intoxicant), place it facing the *jālāmudrā*, and through that opening, while uttering "Hā Phuṃ 2," cast the substance from his mouth into the offering vessel; it should then be offered with the mantra beginning "Oṃ Sarva Kha Kha" and so on. It is to be discarded in a secluded place such as a cremation ground. Thus says the *Karmavajrin*.

"Symbol" (*saṃketa*) is a term that provides a brief exposition; "OṂ" and so forth provide the detailed exposition. Some say that the "mudrā of the three banners" refers to the "symbolic hand. The phrase "after that" refers specifically to the additional *bali* offering during the occasion of the *gaṇacakra*.

Having gathered all the food, side dishes, and so forth contained in various vessels and placed them into a single vessel, one should offer flowers, incense, and the like. Then, the preceptor, his mouth filled with intoxicants, places [the vessel] facing forward with the lattice mudrā; while reciting the syllable *hāḥ puṃ*, he strikes the earthenware bowl situated at its opening with that [mudrā], thereby consecrating the vessel for the *bali* offering.

One should offer [the substance] with the mantra beginning with *oṃ sarva khakhāḥ* and so forth. It should be carried away to a secluded place such as a charnel ground; this is done by the *karmavajra*.

"Compassion" means that the *vajra-gītikā* should be sung during the *gaṇacakra*. To the question of for whom the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth are accomplished, he says "all," and so on; the meaning is: for the yogin who meditates upon the nature of Śrī Saṃvara and Vajravārāhī, which consist of wisdom and method and are composed of great bliss and the purity endowed with all excellent aspects. "Enlightenment" means that one should dedicate the merit produced by the *gaṇacakra* and other practices into suchness, which has the form of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). "Day" means...
The *gaṇacakra* should be performed daily when possible, or monthly if not; however, in its absence, it must certainly be performed every year (*saṃvare*, i.e., *pratisaṃvatsare*). [Note:
An addendum to the *gaṇacakra* paper, pointing out a parallel noted by Wiesiek Mical via email on 25.10.2024:

the meaning is that one should sing vajra songs for the *gaṇacakra* known as "compassion" (*snying rje*). If one asks, "By what means are the activities such as pacification and so forth accomplished? it is said: "In all aspects," and so forth.
The meaning is: "of the yogi who meditates on Śrī Saṃvara and Vajravārāhī, who possess the excellence of all aspects, whose nature is pure great bliss, and who consist of method and wisdom."

Regarding "perfect enlightenment," one should dedicate the merit produced through performing the feast offering (*gaṇacakra*) and so forth—whose nature is the mind of enlightenment—to suchness. As for "every day," if one has the means, the feast offering should be performed daily or monthly; even if one lacks the means, it must certainly be performed once every year.

When the patron has given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, the Lord of the Maṇḍala together with the deities of the maṇḍala should join together and offer auspicious wishes to him with this verse beginning with *saṃsūrya* (meaning *saṃpūjya* or *saṃpūrya*). The syntactical connection is: "May that welfare be yours. What is that? It is "that which" (*yat*), namely "the Wheel was set in motion" (*cakraṃ pravartita*). "Was set in motion" means "you have caused to be turned. In what form? In the form of Ḍākinī, Heruka, and so forth—that is, in the form of Śrī Vajravārāhī, Śrī Saṃvara, and others—having made them the presiding deities.

Regarding the word *jagat*: having fulfilled the desires of the worlds; furthermore, having done what? Having ground the poison of all delusive conceptual constructions (*vikalpa-moha-garala*); having established those to be trained (*vineya*) in the three types of enlightenment according to their capacity; or, having personally attained Buddhahood. "Of the Guru, the Victor" refers to Vajrasattva. "From knowledge" means from non-dual knowledge (*advaya-jñāna*); he whose arising is from that is "this one from knowledge."

The patron, having offered the ritual requisites and so forth, and the lords of the maṇḍala together with the deities of the maṇḍala having assembled, they shall perform virtuous auspicious rites for his sake, using this verse beginning with "Generosity and so forth. This is connected [to the phrase] "May this glorious prosperity be yours. What [things] are these?

"Whoever" refers to anyone who "completely turns the wheel," meaning one who causes it to revolve. In what manner? By way of the ḍākinīs such as Heruka and so forth—that is, in the form of Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, Śrī Vajravārāhī, and the rest. Having done what? Having [fulfilled] "beings"—that is, one should completely fulfill the hopes and aspirations of all beings.

Furthermore, what is to be done? Having destroyed the entire city of conceptual ignorance, and having established those to be trained in the three types of awakening according to their respective capacities, one attains buddhahood oneself—or alternatively, "the Victorious Guru" refers to Vajrasattva. "The Source of Gnosis" (*jñānākara*) refers to non-duality arising from gnosis;
"with this" refers to that very Source of Gnosis.

Having fulfilled the two accumulations through the perfections of generosity and so forth, and having attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, they perform at every moment the boundless welfare of sentient beings in the three realms in the form of the vajra-nature of the maṇḍala of leaders such as Śrī Saṃvara embraced by Śrī Vajravārāhī. The meaning of the verse is: "May you also become like that which is the auspiciousness of the Blessed Lord Śrī Vajrasattva—the collection of qualities such as limitless power and fearlessness, consisting of sovereign majesty."

Having fully perfected the two accumulations through the perfections such as generosity, and having realized unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, one appears in the form of the principal deity of Cakrasaṃvara and so forth, embraced by Vajravārāhī, together with the maṇḍala circle.

The meaning of the verse is: "May it be so for you as well, through the pleasure derived from those who are the very embodiment of great sovereignty—the Blessed Lord Śrī Vajrasattva, who has repeatedly and individually performed the welfare of all sentient beings throughout the three realms without exception, and who possesses a collection of peerless qualities such as the powers and fearlessnesses."
Thus ends the commentary on the thirty-second chapter. || 0 ||
This is the explanation of the thirty-second chapter.
